title: EU Digital Fairness Act Targets Addictive AI Features
summary: New EU regulation requires social media platforms to allow users to disable addictive features and AI chatbots. Meta, Google, TikTok face 6% revenue fines.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- EU's Digital Fairness Act mandates user controls for addictive social media features and relationship-simulating AI chatbots.
- Meta, Google, and TikTok face potential fines up to 6% of global revenue for non-compliance.
- Draft presented November 9, 2026, complements existing Digital Services Act investigations into platform design practices.


The European Union officially presented the Digital Fairness Act on November 9, 2026, introducing sweeping new requirements for social media platforms and AI systems. The regulation mandates that companies provide adult users with controls to disable features designed to encourage compulsive usage, including AI chatbots that simulate personal relationships to drive continued engagement.


## Regulatory Requirements and Penalties


Under the draft legislation seen by Bloomberg News, technology companies must allow users to switch off algorithmic features that promote excessive platform use. The rules specifically target AI systems engineered to create parasocial bonds with users, a growing concern as conversational AI becomes more sophisticated. Companies failing to comply face fines reaching 6% of their worldwide annual revenue, representing one of the strictest penalty structures in global tech regulation.


The regulation affects major platforms including Meta Platforms, Alphabet's Google, and ByteDance's TikTok. These services rely heavily on engagement optimization features that keep users active for extended periods, making compliance a significant operational challenge.


## Release Date and Implementation Timeline


Officially launched on November 9, 2026, the Digital Fairness Act complements the European Commission's existing Digital Services Act enforcement framework. Both Meta and TikTok are currently under investigation for suspected addictive design practices under DSA provisions. The new legislation expands regulatory scope beyond content moderation to address the fundamental architecture of user engagement systems.


The commission has not specified an implementation deadline, but platforms typically receive 12 to 18 months for compliance with major EU digital regulations.


## AI Chatbot and Relationship Simulation Provisions


A distinctive element of the Digital Fairness Act addresses AI systems that simulate emotional connections with users. These provisions respond to emerging patterns in conversational AI deployment, where chatbots increasingly adopt personas designed to foster attachment and repeated interaction. The regulation requires transparent disclosure when AI systems employ relationship-building techniques and mandates user controls to limit such interactions.


Industry observers note this represents the first major regulatory framework explicitly addressing parasocial AI relationships at scale. The rules could reshape how companies design companion chatbots and virtual assistants.


## Coordinated Youth Protection Measures


The Digital Fairness Act operates alongside the EU's forthcoming Kids Act, which will impose "safe by design" requirements on social networks and AI platforms. The Kids Act includes provisions restricting social media access for young teenagers, creating a comprehensive regulatory approach spanning all age groups.


- Mandatory opt-out controls for addictive features
- Disclosure requirements for AI relationship simulation
- 6% global revenue penalty cap for violations
- Coordination with Digital Services Act enforcement
- Integration with youth protection framework


## What This Means


The Digital Fairness Act marks a fundamental shift in how European regulators approach platform design. Rather than focusing solely on content moderation, the EU now directly targets the engagement mechanics underlying modern social media and AI systems. For global technology companies, this creates new compliance obligations that may influence product development worldwide, as regional regulatory standards often cascade into global design practices. The regulation's AI chatbot provisions also signal regulatory awareness of emerging risks in conversational AI, establishing a precedent other jurisdictions may follow as relationship-simulating systems become more prevalent.
